settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The class is named a 'Default' resolver and an ExactMatchRedirectResolver subclass exists, so deployments can opt into strict equality.
When registered redirect URIs ARE provided by the client, the value returned is the matching registered/requested URI and unregistered targets are rejected via RedirectMismatchException (line 159).
For a single registered redirect URI and a null requestedRedirect, the registered value is returned (line 151-152), which is safe.
candidates.description: DefaultRedirectResolver.resolveRedirect implements the redirect_uri authorization check. It throws a RedirectMismatchException only when the client has registered redirect URIs AND none of them match. If the client's registered redirect set is null or empty, the method simply returns the raw requestedRedirect supplied by the (unauthenticated) requester (line 79-81). It also, when registered URIs exist, returns the raw requested value whenever redirectMatches is true (obtainMatchingRedirect, line 155-156). This means for clients configured without a fixed redirect URI (or for which nothing is registered), an attacker controlling the authorize request can choose an arbitrary redirect target. The registered URI is the primary defense against authorization-code / access-token leakage and against open redirects, so trusting the attacker-supplied value is a security-relevant weakening. The default resolver is the one instantiated at AuthorizationEndpoint line 94, so this is the default behavior of the authorization server unless an administrator overrides it.
missing_evidence: No evidence that any in-repo configuration registers a client without redirect URIs; no real deployment config was inspected.
No test or documentation demonstrating attacker-controlled exploitation.
The default client registration path (BaseClientDetails) and whether it can produce an empty redirect set was not fully traced.
preconditions: A client is registered with an empty/null registered redirect URI set (redirectUris empty) but is allowed to use an implicit or authorization_code grant.
The attacker (or victim) initiates /oauth/authorize with an attacker-chosen redirect_uri.
The default DefaultRedirectResolver is in use (AuthorizationEndpoint line 94) rather than ExactMatchRedirectResolver.
candidates.title: DefaultRedirectResolver trusts unregistered client-supplied redirect_uri (open redirect / code & token exposure)

counter_evidence: The behavior is documented in the Javadoc (lines 102-106) as intentional design.
An ExactMatchRedirectResolver exists for strict comparison.
The protocol equality check limits matching to the same scheme.
candidates.description: DefaultRedirectResolver.redirectMatches accepts a requested redirect if the protocol is equal, the host matches via hostMatches (which, with the default matchSubdomains=true, checks only requested.endsWith(registered)), and the cleaned requested path starts with the cleaned registered path. The Javadoc explicitly states 'the port is not matched'. Two consequences are security-relevant: (a) with matchSubdomains enabled, a registered host like 'example.com' also matches attacker-controlled hosts that merely end with that string (e.g. 'evilexample.com'), because endsWith is a raw suffix test rather than a label-aware comparison; (b) because the path check is a prefix test and the port/host are not strictly compared, redirect targets can resolve to an unintended origin/path. These looseness properties make the redirect target less tightly bound to the registered client, which matters for code/token delivery.
missing_evidence: No concrete deployment/registration example showing a registered URI that an attacker suffix or path-prefix can collide with.
No test exercising matchSubdomains with adversarial host values was read.
preconditions: A client registers one or more redirect URIs that are full URLs.
matchSubdomains is left at its default true (line 43), or a registered path is a prefix of an attacker path.
The attacker can choose/supply the redirect_uri on /oauth/authorize.
candidates.title: DefaultRedirectResolver redirect matching uses host suffix, path prefix and ignores port

counter_evidence: WhitelabelErrorEndpoint explicitly escapes its error summary with HtmlUtils.htmlEscape (lines 27-32), showing the project is aware of the XSS risk in this rendering path and mitigates it there.
The SpelView templates in WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint are static constants; only the interpolated values are dynamic.
Default framework behavior constrains scopes to client-registered values in typical configurations, limiting attacker control of scope names.
candidates.description: SpelView.render builds the HTML view by taking the template and running it through a PropertyPlaceholderHelper whose PlaceholderResolver parses each ${...} placeholder as a SpEL expression and evaluates it against the model map (lines 51-57, 70-71). The resulting string is written directly to the response with contentType text/html and no output encoding (lines 72-73). WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint builds its template from model/request data without escaping: createScopes interpolates the raw scope name into the SCOPE HTML fragment via %scope% and %key% (lines 54-55, 71-72), and the model (including 'scopes') is populated from request-derived data (lines 21-26, 31-33). If scope values are attacker-influenced, the rendered approval page reflects them unencoded. Separately, because placeholder values are evaluated as SpEL against a StandardEvaluationContext rooted at the model, any template value that is itself interpretable as a SpEL expression is evaluated; while the templates here are constants, this design makes the rendering sensitive to unescaped/untrusted model content.
missing_evidence: No trace proving an attacker can place arbitrary strings into the 'scopes' map that reaches WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint's template.
No in-repo test or advisory confirming an exploitation path.
Whether the default OAuth2 request factory rejects unknown scopes before the approval page is rendered was not fully verified.
preconditions: The whitelabel approval endpoint (/oauth/confirm_access) is in use and returns SpelView.
Scope names (or other interpolated model values) can be influenced by the requester, e.g. via an unrecognized/forged scope parameter reaching the approval page model.
The response is rendered without an additional escaping layer/Content-Security-Policy.
candidates.title: SpelView evaluates resolved placeholder content as SpEL and the approval page does not HTML-escape scopes
